title: Water already in your house
summary: When the water stops or turns unsafe, shut the main valve, then use the water in your pipes, water heater, ice and toilet tank; never drink from radiators, boilers, waterbeds or pools.
doFirst: Broken water or sewer lines, or told the water is unsafe? Shut the main water valve now.
Warned that the water will go off? Fill clean containers, large pots, sinks and bathtubs while it still runs.
Before you drain the water heater, turn its electricity or gas off and let it cool.
Don’t drink from radiators, boilers, waterbeds, pools, spas or the toilet bowl.

blocks.p: Find your incoming water valve now, before you need it (FEMA). It is where the water pipe enters the house.
Shut it if you hear of broken water or sewer lines, or if officials say there is a problem. This stops contaminated water getting into the pipes in your house (FEMA, CDC).

steps: With the main valve shut, turn on the tap on the highest floor of the house to let air into the pipes. A small amount of water will trickle out.
Then take water from the lowest tap in the house.

blocks.p: Steps from FEMA, the Red Cross and USDA.

Use the tank that feeds your hot taps and showers, not the tank that feeds radiators in older homes (CDC). Use it only if it is not damaged (FEMA and Red Cross). An on-demand (tankless) heater does not hold a tank of water (Regional Water Providers Consortium).

blocks.warn: Do these steps in this order. The power or gas must be off before you open the drain. The water may be very hot: wear gloves and eye protection (Regional Water Providers Consortium).

steps: Make sure the electricity or gas to the water heater is off (FEMA).
Let the tank cool (Louisiana emergency preparedness office).
Close the water intake valve, usually on top of the tank: turn it clockwise until it stops (Regional Water Providers Consortium).
Turn on a hot-water tap in the house to let air into the tank (Regional Water Providers Consortium, FEMA).
Put a clean container under the drain valve at the bottom of the tank (Louisiana, Regional Water Providers Consortium).
Open the drain at the bottom of the tank (FEMA).

Do not turn on the gas or electricity while the tank is empty (FEMA). When the water supply is back, close the drain and refill the tank following the heater’s instructions before you turn the power or gas back on. For a gas heater, follow the heater’s or the gas company’s instructions to relight it.

blocks.cap: Do the steps in this order: power or gas off, let the tank cool, close the water intake valve, open a hot tap, put a container under the drain valve, open the drain. Refill the tank before you turn the power or gas back on.

list: Melted ice cubes made with water that was not contaminated (CDC, FEMA). Keep the ice in a clean place.
Liquid from canned fruit and vegetables (CDC, FEMA).

The toilet tank (the tank behind the seat, never the bowl), only if the water is clear and has no toilet cleaner in it: no colored water, no tablet or hanging cleaner (CDC, FEMA, University of Alaska Fairbanks Extension). FEMA calls it a last resort. Treat it before you drink it.
If you are warned before the water goes off, fill large pots, sinks and bathtubs (Ohio State University Extension). Treat sink and bathtub water before you drink it.

blocks.p: CDC counts water from the heater tank, clean ice, a clear untreated toilet tank and canned food liquid as clean and safe. FEMA and the Red Cross say water needs treating only if you are not sure it is pure.
Treat it if you are not sure: if the water was under a boil-water notice, if lines broke before you shut the valve, if it looks or smells wrong, or if you don’t know.

head: Water
Drink it?
Other use
rows: Radiators and hot-water boilers (the home heating system)
Don’t use it: fungicides added to the water and chemicals in the vinyl may make it unsafe (FEMA).
Washing yourself, cleaning and similar uses (CDC, FEMA).

sources.name: FEMA, American Red Cross and USDA, Food and Water in an Emergency
sources.used: Know the incoming water valve; shut it to stop contaminated water entering if you hear of broken water or sewage lines; pipes: highest faucet to let in air, a little trickles out, then the lowest faucet; hot-water tank: electricity or gas off, open the drain at the bottom, start the flow by turning off the water intake valve and turning on a hot-water faucet, do not turn on gas or electricity when the tank is empty; ice cubes; toilet reservoir tank as a last resort, not the bowl; do not drink floodwater

sources.name: CDC, How to Find Clean Water in an Emergency (reviewed June 25, 2025)
sources.used: Tap water heater tank, not the tank supplying radiators in older homes; melted ice made with uncontaminated water; toilet tank not the bowl, if clear and not treated with toilet cleaners such as those that change the color of the water; liquid from canned fruit and vegetables; pool and spa water for hygiene and cleaning, not drinking; shut the main water valve to keep contaminants out of your pipes

sources.name: FEMA, Fact Sheet: How to Make Your Water Safe to Drink (October 8, 2017)
sources.used: Water heater tank (drinking water system, not heating system); melted uncontaminated ice; toilet tank not bowl, clear and untreated; canned fruit and vegetable liquid; pools and spas for hygiene and cleaning, not drinking; sources not to use: radiators, hot water boilers, waterbeds (fungicides and vinyl chemicals); shut off the main water valve

sources.name: FEMA, Where can I find clean drinking water after a disaster?
sources.used: Do not drink water from radiators or boilers in a home heating system, or from swimming pools and spas; keep the ice storage area clean

sources.name: Regional Water Providers Consortium, How to access water from your water heater during an emergency (water heater hanger, 2022)
sources.used: Turn off the heater’s water supply at the shut-off valve usually on top of the tank, clockwise until it stops; let air in by opening a hot water faucet; clean container under the drain valve; the water may be very hot, gloves and safety glasses recommended; for gas heaters it says to set the knob to pilot (the app follows FEMA: off)

sources.name: Keep This With Your Water Heater (flyer, no publisher printed; hosted by Eugene Water & Electric Board)
sources.used: Shut off the water supply, cut power, let air in by running hot water, then drain into a clean container; wear gloves and eye protection; follow the manufacturer’s instructions when refilling the tank; gas heaters: see the gas utility’s safety measures

sources.name: Regional Water Providers Consortium, Emergency Water Sources
sources.used: Tankless heaters hold no tank of water; Do Not Drink: toilet bowl or tank, radiators, water beds (starred: may be sanitation sources), pool, hot tub, flood water

sources.name: Louisiana Governor’s Office of Homeland Security and Emergency Preparedness, Locating Safe Drinking Water
sources.used: Hot-water tank: turn off the power that heats it and let the tank cool, place a container underneath, open the drain valve at the bottom, don’t turn the tank on again until water services are restored

sources.name: National Disaster Education Coalition (American Red Cross, FEMA and others), Talking About Disaster: Disaster Supplies Kit
sources.used: Use water from undamaged hot water tanks, toilet tanks (not the bowl) and water pipes; water needs to be treated only if it is of questionable purity

sources.name: University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension, Emergency Water Supply (SAL-00006, 2021)
sources.used: Toilet tank water only without a hanging deodorizer or other chemicals; tank storage in heaters that are not on-demand

sources.name: Ohio State University Extension, Preserving Water for Emergency Use (HYG-5354, 2017)
sources.used: If warned ahead of time, fill large pots and pans, sinks and bathtubs
